questions.question:
The displacement of a particle is given by
$$x=\frac{e^{2t}-e^{-2t}}{2}.$$
The acceleration of the particle is
questions.answer: $\dot x=\dfrac{2e^{2t}+2e^{-2t}}{2}$, so $\ddot x=\dfrac{4e^{2t}-4e^{-2t}}{2}=4\left(\dfrac{e^{2t}-e^{-2t}}{2}\right)=4x$. The acceleration is four times the displacement, in the same direction (C).
options: Twice the displacement in the same direction
Twice the displacement in the opposite direction
Four times the displacement in the same direction
Four times the displacement in the opposite direction

questions.question:
Which of the following is the negation of the statement

"If I know how to negate this statement, then I will select the correct answer"?
questions.answer: The negation of $P\Rightarrow Q$ is $P\wedge\neg Q$: "I know how to negate this statement and I will not select the correct answer" (B).
options: If I don't know how to negate this statement, then I will not select the correct answer
I know how to negate this statement and I will not select the correct answer
If I do not select the correct answer, then I do not know how to negate this statement
I do not know how to negate this statement and I will select the correct answer

questions.question:
For the complex number $z=a+ib$, which of the following is the correct expression for
$$\sum_{k=0}^{2025} i^{k}z\ ?$$
questions.answer: Write $\sum_{k=0}^{2025}i^kz=(i^0+i^1)z+\sum_{k=2}^{2025}i^kz$. The last sum has $2024$ terms, a multiple of $4$, and any four consecutive powers of $i$ sum to $0$, so it vanishes. Hence the sum is $(1+i)(a+ib)=a+ib+ia-b=(a-b)+(a+b)i$ (B).

questions.question:
Using the substitution $u=1+e^{x}$,
$$\int_0^{\ln 2}\frac{1}{1+e^{x}}\,dx$$
can be expressed as
questions.answer: $du=e^x\,dx$, so $dx=\dfrac{du}{u-1}$. When $x=0$, $u=2$; when $x=\ln2$, $u=3$. Then $\displaystyle\int_2^3\frac{1}{u(u-1)}\,du$ and $\dfrac{1}{u(u-1)}=\dfrac{1}{u-1}-\dfrac1u$, giving $\displaystyle\int_2^3\left(\frac1{u-1}-\frac1u\right)du$ (B).

questions.question: For the vectors $\mathbf{p}=\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\\c\end{pmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{q}=\begin{pmatrix}b\\c\\a\end{pmatrix}$, which of the following is the expression for $\left|\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{p}\right|$?
questions.answer: $\left|\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf q}\mathbf p\right|=\dfrac{|\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q|}{|\mathbf q|}=\dfrac{|ab+bc+ca|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}}$ (D).

questions.question: Let $a$ and $b$ be real numbers with $a\ne b$. Let $z=x+iy$ be a complex number such that $|z-a|^2-|z-b|^2=1$. Which of the following best describes the locus of $z$?
questions.answer: $(x-a)^2+y^2-\left[(x-b)^2+y^2\right]=1\Rightarrow 2(b-a)x+a^2-b^2=1$, so $x=\dfrac{1+b^2-a^2}{2(b-a)}$, a constant (as $a\neq b$). The locus is a vertical line (D).

questions.question:
Two particles with masses $m_1$ kilograms and $m_2$ kilograms are connected by a taut light string that passes over a smooth pulley. The particles sit on smooth inclined planes, inclined at $2\theta$ and $\theta$ to the horizontal, as shown in the diagram.

If the system is in equilibrium, then $\dfrac{m_1}{m_2}$ is equal to
questions.answer: Along each smooth plane the tension balances the component of weight down the plane: $T=m_1g\sin2\theta$ and $T=m_2g\sin\theta$. Hence $\dfrac{m_1}{m_2}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\sin2\theta}=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\dfrac1{2\cos\theta}=\dfrac{\sec\theta}{2}$ (A).

questions.question:
How many ordered pairs of positive real numbers $(a,b)$ exist that satisfy the equation
$$(1+2a)(2+2b)(2a+b)=32ab\ ?$$
questions.answer: By AM-GM: $1+2a\ge2\sqrt{2a}$, $2+2b\ge2\sqrt{4b}$, $2a+b\ge2\sqrt{2ab}$. Multiplying, $(1+2a)(2+2b)(2a+b)\ge8\sqrt{16a^2b^2}=32ab$. Equality holds only if $1=2a$, $2=2b$ and $2a=b$, i.e. $a=\tfrac12$, $b=1$ (consistent in all three). So there is exactly one pair, $(\tfrac12,1)$ (B).

questions.question:
Points $P$ and $Q$ have position vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ respectively. The expression
$$\frac12\sqrt{|\mathbf{p}|^2|\mathbf{q}|^2-(\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{q})^2}$$
is an expression for
questions.answer: With $\mathbf p\cdot\mathbf q=|\mathbf p||\mathbf q|\cos\theta$: $\tfrac12\sqrt{|\mathbf p|^2|\mathbf q|^2(1-\cos^2\theta)}=\tfrac12|\mathbf p||\mathbf q|\sin\theta$, which is the area of $\triangle OPQ$ (B).
options: The magnitude of the position vector of the midpoint of $PQ$

questions.question: For complex numbers $z$ satisfying $|1+z+z^2|=4$, the maximum magnitude of the imaginary part of $z$ can be written as $\dfrac{\sqrt m}{n}$. What is $m+n$?
questions.answer: Complete the square: $1+z+z^2=\left(z+\tfrac12\right)^2+\tfrac34$. Let $u=z+\tfrac12$, which has the same imaginary part as $z$. Then $|u^2+\tfrac34|=4$, so $u^2$ lies on the circle with centre $-\tfrac34$ and radius $4$, whose farthest point from the origin is $u^2=-\tfrac{19}4$, so $|u^2|\le\tfrac{19}4$. Since $\operatorname{Im}z=\operatorname{Im}u$ and $|\operatorname{Im}u|\le|u|=\sqrt{|u^2|}\le\dfrac{\sqrt{19}}2$, with equality when $u=\pm\tfrac{\sqrt{19}}2i$ (then $u^2=-\tfrac{19}4$), the maximum is $\dfrac{\sqrt{19}}2$. So $m+n=19+2=21$ (C).

questions.question:
What is the contrapositive of the statement

"For any integers $a$ and $b$, $a+b\ge15$ implies that $a\ge8$ or $b\ge8$"?
questions.answer: The contrapositive of $P\Rightarrow Q$ is $\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$: "For any integers $a$ and $b$, $a<8$ and $b<8$ implies that $a+b<15$."

questions.question: Prove that for any integers $a$ and $b$, if $a+b\ge15$ then $a\ge8$ or $b\ge8$, by proving its contrapositive: for any integers $a$ and $b$, $a<8$ and $b<8$ implies that $a+b<15$.
questions.answer: Since $a$ and $b$ are integers, $a<8\Rightarrow a\le7$ and $b<8\Rightarrow b\le7$. Hence $a+b\le14<15$. The contrapositive is true, so the original statement is true (an implication is equivalent to its contrapositive).

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int x\sin x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Integrate by parts with $u=x$, $v'=\sin x$ ($u'=1$, $v=-\cos x$):
$$\int x\sin x\,dx=-x\cos x+\int\cos x\,dx=-x\cos x+\sin x+C.$$

questions.question: Show that $x=2i$ is a solution to $x^4-2x^3+8x^2-8x+16=0$.
Given that $x=2i$ is a root of $P(x)=x^4-2x^3+8x^2-8x+16$, express $P(x)$ as a product of two quadratic factors (with real coefficients).
questions.answer:
$P$ has real coefficients, so $x=-2i$ is also a root (conjugate root theorem). Thus $(x-2i)(x+2i)=x^2+4$ is a factor. Dividing, $P(x)\div(x^2+4)=x^2-2x+4$ (check: $(x^2+4)(x^2-2x+4)=x^4-2x^3+8x^2-8x+16$). So
$$P(x)=(x^2+4)(x^2-2x+4).$$

questions.question: Given that $P(x)=x^4-2x^3+8x^2-8x+16=(x^2+4)(x^2-2x+4)$, express $P(x)$ as the product of four linear factors.
questions.answer:
$x^2+4=(x-2i)(x+2i)$. For $x^2-2x+4=0$: $x=\dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4-16}}{2}=1\pm\sqrt3\,i$. Hence
$$P(x)=(x-2i)(x+2i)\left(x-1-\sqrt3 i\right)\left(x-1+\sqrt3 i\right).$$

questions.question: Points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are defined by position vectors $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{b}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{c}=p\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}$, where $p$ is a real constant. Given that $\angle ABC=\dfrac\pi3$, find the value(s) of $p$.
questions.answer:
$\overrightarrow{BA}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}p-2\\-1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$, so $|\overrightarrow{BA}|=\sqrt2$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|=\sqrt{p^2-4p+6}$ and $\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=-(p-2)-1=1-p$.

From $\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=|\overrightarrow{BA}||\overrightarrow{BC}|\cos\frac\pi3$:
$$1-p=\tfrac12\sqrt2\sqrt{p^2-4p+6}.$$
The right side is positive so $p<1$. Squaring: $(1-p)^2=\tfrac14\cdot2(p^2-4p+6)\Rightarrow 2-4p+2p^2=p^2-4p+6\Rightarrow p^2=4$, so $p=\pm2$. As $p<1$, $p=-2$.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/3}(\sec x\tan x)^3\,dx$.
questions.answer:
$$(\sec x\tan x)^3=\sec x\tan x\cdot\sec^2x\tan^2x=\sec x\tan x\sec^2x(\sec^2x-1)=\sec^4x\cdot\sec x\tan x-\sec^2x\cdot\sec x\tan x.$$
Since $\frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x$,
$$\int_0^{\pi/3}=\left[\frac{\sec^5x}{5}-\frac{\sec^3x}{3}\right]_0^{\pi/3}=\left(\frac{32}{5}-\frac83\right)-\left(\frac15-\frac13\right)=\frac{31}{5}-\frac73=\frac{58}{15}.$$

questions.question:
The displacement, from origin $O$, of a small statue caught in a tornado is given by the vector
$$\mathbf{r}=\left(50+25\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{i}+\left(50+25\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{j}+\frac{2t}{5}\mathbf{k}$$
where $\mathbf{i}$ is a unit vector East, $\mathbf{j}$ a unit vector North and $\mathbf{k}$ a unit vector vertically up. Displacement components are in metres and time $t$ is in seconds.

Find the time, in seconds, for the statue to reach a height of $60$ m.
questions.answer: Height is the $\mathbf k$ component: $\dfrac{2t}{5}=60\Rightarrow t=150$ seconds.

questions.question:
The displacement, from origin $O$, of a small statue caught in a tornado is given by the vector
$$\mathbf{r}=\left(50+25\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{i}+\left(50+25\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{j}+\frac{2t}{5}\mathbf{k}$$
where $\mathbf{i}$ is a unit vector East, $\mathbf{j}$ a unit vector North and $\mathbf{k}$ a unit vector vertically up. Displacement components are in metres and time $t$ is in seconds.

Find, to the nearest degree, the angle of elevation from $O$ of the statue when it is at a height of $60$ m.
questions.answer:
At $t=150$: $\frac{\pi t}{30}=5\pi$, so $x=50+25\cos5\pi=25$, $y=50+25\sin5\pi=50$, $z=60$. The horizontal distance from $O$ is $\sqrt{25^2+50^2}$, so
$$\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{60}{\sqrt{25^2+50^2}}\right)\approx47^\circ.$$

questions.question:
The displacement, from origin $O$, of a small statue caught in a tornado is given by the vector
$$\mathbf{r}=\left(50+25\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{i}+\left(50+25\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{j}+\frac{2t}{5}\mathbf{k}$$
where $\mathbf{i}$ is a unit vector East, $\mathbf{j}$ a unit vector North and $\mathbf{k}$ a unit vector vertically up. Displacement components are in metres and time $t$ is in seconds.

After how many seconds will the statue first be directly above its original point on the surface of the planet?
questions.answer: The horizontal position $(50+25\cos\frac{\pi t}{30},\,50+25\sin\frac{\pi t}{30})$ returns to its initial value after one period $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/30}=60$ seconds.

questions.question:
The displacement, from origin $O$, of a small statue caught in a tornado is given by the vector
$$\mathbf{r}=\left(50+25\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{i}+\left(50+25\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{j}+\frac{2t}{5}\mathbf{k}$$
where $\mathbf{i}$ is a unit vector East, $\mathbf{j}$ a unit vector North and $\mathbf{k}$ a unit vector vertically up. Displacement components are in metres and time $t$ is in seconds.

Show that the velocity of the statue is perpendicular to its acceleration.
questions.answer:
$$\mathbf v=\dot{\mathbf r}=-\frac{5\pi}{6}\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\,\mathbf i+\frac{5\pi}{6}\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}\,\mathbf j+\frac25\mathbf k,\qquad \mathbf a=\dot{\mathbf v}=-\frac{\pi^2}{36}\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}\,\mathbf i-\frac{\pi^2}{36}\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\,\mathbf j.$$
$$\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v=\frac{5\pi^3}{216}\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}-\frac{5\pi^3}{216}\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}+\frac25\cdot0=0.$$
Hence $\mathbf v\perp\mathbf a$.

questions.question:
The displacement, from origin $O$, of a small statue caught in a tornado is given by the vector
$$\mathbf{r}=\left(50+25\cos\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{i}+\left(50+25\sin\frac{\pi t}{30}\right)\mathbf{j}+\frac{2t}{5}\mathbf{k}$$
where $\mathbf{i}$ is a unit vector East, $\mathbf{j}$ a unit vector North and $\mathbf{k}$ a unit vector vertically up. Displacement components are in metres and time $t$ is in seconds.

Find the speed, in metres per second, at which the statue is travelling. Answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.answer: Let $\theta=\frac{\pi t}{30}$. $|\mathbf v|^2=\frac{25\pi^2}{36}(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)+\frac4{25}=\frac{25\pi^2}{36}+\frac{4}{25}\approx7.01$. So the speed is constant: $\approx2.65$ m s$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Let $\omega$ be a non-real root of the equation $z^3+8=0$. Show that $\omega^2=2\omega-4$.
questions.answer: $z^3+8=(z+2)(z^2-2z+4)=0$. Since $\omega$ is a root, $(\omega+2)(\omega^2-2\omega+4)=0$. As $\omega$ is non-real, $\omega\ne-2$, so $\omega^2-2\omega+4=0$, i.e. $\omega^2=2\omega-4$.

questions.question: Let $\omega$ be a non-real root of $z^3+8=0$, so that $\omega^2=2\omega-4$. Hence evaluate $(2\omega-4)^6$.

Prove that for $a,b,c>0$,
$$\frac{a^2}{b^3c}-\frac{a}{b^2}\ge\frac cb-\frac{c^2}{a}.$$
questions.answer:
Over the common denominator $ab^3c$:
$$\frac{a^2}{b^3c}-\frac a{b^2}-\frac cb+\frac{c^2}a=\frac{a^3-a^2bc-ab^2c^2+b^3c^3}{ab^3c}=\frac{a^2(a-bc)-b^2c^2(a-bc)}{ab^3c}=\frac{(a-bc)(a^2-b^2c^2)}{ab^3c}=\frac{(a-bc)^2(a+bc)}{ab^3c}.$$
For $a,b,c>0$ this is $\ge0$, so LHS $\ge$ RHS.

questions.question:
For $a,b,c>0$ it is known that
$$\frac{a^2}{b^3c}-\frac{a}{b^2}-\left(\frac cb-\frac{c^2}{a}\right)=\frac{(a-bc)^2(a+bc)}{ab^3c}\ge0.$$
Under what conditions does equality occur in $\dfrac{a^2}{b^3c}-\dfrac{a}{b^2}\ge\dfrac cb-\dfrac{c^2}{a}$?
questions.answer: Equality holds when $(a-bc)^2(a+bc)=0$. As $a+bc>0$, this requires $a=bc$.

questions.question: Use partial fractions to find $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{x^2(x-1)}$.
questions.answer:
Write $\dfrac{1}{x^2(x-1)}=\dfrac{A}{x-1}+\dfrac Bx+\dfrac C{x^2}$, so $1=Ax^2+Bx(x-1)+C(x-1)=(A+B)x^2+(C-B)x-C$. Then $C=-1$, $B=-1$, $A=1$.
$$\int\frac{dx}{x^2(x-1)}=\int\left(\frac1{x-1}-\frac1x-\frac1{x^2}\right)dx=\ln|x-1|-\ln|x|+\frac1x+C.$$

questions.question: Use the substitution $t=\tan\dfrac\theta2$ to find $\displaystyle\int\operatorname{cosec}\theta\,d\theta$.
questions.answer:
With $t=\tan\frac\theta2$: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$ and $d\theta=\dfrac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$. Then
$$\int\operatorname{cosec}\theta\,d\theta=\int\frac{1+t^2}{2t}\cdot\frac{2}{1+t^2}\,dt=\int\frac1t\,dt=\ln|t|+C=\ln\left|\tan\frac\theta2\right|+C.$$

questions.question:
$OABC$ is a parallelogram drawn on the Argand plane such that $O$ is the origin, $A$ is represented by the complex number $w$ and $C$ by the complex number $z$. Squares are constructed outwards on each of the four sides of the parallelogram, with centres $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ (on sides $OA$, $AB$, $BC$ and $CO$ respectively) as shown.

Show that $\overrightarrow{PR}$ is given by the complex number $z+iw$.
questions.answer:
Let $D$ be the midpoint of $OA$ and $F$ the midpoint of $BC$. $P$ is the centre of the square on $OA$, so $\overrightarrow{DP}$ is half of $\overrightarrow{OA}=w$ rotated by $-90^\circ$: $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac12w-\tfrac12iw$. Similarly $\overrightarrow{CF}=\tfrac12w$, and $\overrightarrow{FR}$ is half of $\overrightarrow{CB}=w$ rotated by $+90^\circ$: $\overrightarrow{OR}=z+\tfrac12w+\tfrac12iw$. Then
$$\overrightarrow{PR}=\overrightarrow{OR}-\overrightarrow{OP}=z+\tfrac12w+\tfrac12iw-\tfrac12w+\tfrac12iw=z+iw.$$

questions.question:
$OABC$ is a parallelogram drawn on the Argand plane such that $O$ is the origin, $A$ is represented by the complex number $w$ and $C$ by the complex number $z$. Squares are constructed outwards on each of the four sides of the parallelogram, with centres $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ (on sides $OA$, $AB$, $BC$ and $CO$ respectively) as shown.

Find a similar expression in terms of $w$, $z$ and $i$ for $\overrightarrow{QS}$.
questions.answer:
Let $E$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and $G$ the midpoint of $CO$. $\overrightarrow{AB}=z$, so $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AE}+\overrightarrow{EQ}=w+\tfrac12z-\tfrac12iz$. Also $\overrightarrow{OS}=\overrightarrow{OG}+\overrightarrow{GS}=\tfrac12z+\tfrac12iz$. Therefore
$$\overrightarrow{QS}=\overrightarrow{OS}-\overrightarrow{OQ}=\tfrac12z+\tfrac12iz-w-\tfrac12z+\tfrac12iz=iz-w.$$

questions.question:
$OABC$ is a parallelogram drawn on the Argand plane such that $O$ is the origin, $A$ is represented by the complex number $w$ and $C$ by the complex number $z$. Squares are constructed outwards on each of the four sides of the parallelogram, with centres $P$, $Q$, $R$ and $S$ (on sides $OA$, $AB$, $BC$ and $CO$ respectively) as shown.

Given that $\overrightarrow{PR}=z+iw$ and $\overrightarrow{QS}=iz-w$, show that $PQRS$ is a square.
questions.answer: $i\overrightarrow{PR}=iz+i^2w=iz-w=\overrightarrow{QS}$, so the diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ are equal in length and perpendicular (rotation by $90^\circ$). The midpoint of $PR$ is $\tfrac12(\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OR})=\tfrac12(w+z)$ and the midpoint of $QS$ is $\tfrac12(\overrightarrow{OQ}+\overrightarrow{OS})=\tfrac12(w+\tfrac12z-\tfrac12iz+\tfrac12z+\tfrac12iz)=\tfrac12(w+z)$, so the diagonals bisect each other. A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal, perpendicular and bisect each other is a square.

questions.question:
Find the points of intersection between the sphere
$$x^2+y^2+z^2-4x+2y-6z+5=0$$
and the line
$$\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}7\\-1\\9\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}.$$
questions.answer:
Completing the square: $(x-2)^2+(y+1)^2+(z-3)^2=9$. On the line, $x=7+3\lambda$, $y=-1-\lambda$, $z=9+4\lambda$:
$$(5+3\lambda)^2+\lambda^2+(6+4\lambda)^2=9\Rightarrow26\lambda^2+78\lambda+52=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2+3\lambda+2=0,$$
so $\lambda=-1$ or $\lambda=-2$. The points of intersection are $(4,0,5)$ and $(1,1,1)$.

questions.question: A particle moves in a straight line with acceleration $a=2x^3+2x$ metres per second squared, where $x$ is its displacement in metres. It starts at the origin with an initial velocity of $1$ m s$^{-1}$. Find its velocity in terms of displacement.
questions.answer:
$v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=2x(x^2+1)$, so $\displaystyle\int_1^v v\,dv=\int_0^x2x(x^2+1)\,dx$:
$$\tfrac12v^2-\tfrac12=\tfrac12(x^2+1)^2-\tfrac12\Rightarrow v^2=(x^2+1)^2.$$
Since $v\ne0$ for all $x$ and the initial velocity is positive, $v=x^2+1$.

questions.question: A particle moves in a straight line, starting at the origin at $t=0$. Its velocity in terms of its displacement $x$ is $v=x^2+1$. Find its displacement in terms of time.
questions.answer: $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=x^2+1\Rightarrow\displaystyle\int_0^t dt=\int_0^x\frac{dx}{1+x^2}\Rightarrow t=\tan^{-1}x$. Hence $x=\tan t$.

questions.question:
A parallelepiped is a three-dimensional figure formed by six parallelograms; opposite faces are identical. Consider the parallelepiped $OABCDEFG$ shown, where $O$ is adjacent to $A$, $C$ and $D$.

Prove that the diagonals $OF$ and $CE$ bisect each other.
questions.answer:
Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$, $\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$, $\overrightarrow{OD}=\mathbf d$. Opposite edges are equal: $\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OC}=\mathbf c$, $\overrightarrow{BF}=\overrightarrow{OD}=\mathbf d$, $\overrightarrow{DE}=\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$.

Let $X$ be the midpoint of $OF$: $\overrightarrow{OX}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{OF}=\tfrac12(\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BF})=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c+\mathbf d)$.

Let $Y$ be the midpoint of $CE$: $\overrightarrow{OY}=\overrightarrow{OC}+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{CE}=\tfrac12(\overrightarrow{OC}+\overrightarrow{OE})=\tfrac12(\mathbf c+\overrightarrow{OD}+\overrightarrow{DE})=\tfrac12(\mathbf c+\mathbf d+\mathbf a)$.

So $X$ and $Y$ coincide: the diagonals bisect each other.

questions.question:
A parallelepiped is a three-dimensional figure formed by six parallelograms; opposite faces are identical. Consider the parallelepiped $OABCDEFG$ shown, where $O$ is adjacent to $A$, $C$ and $D$.

Let $M$ be the midpoint of $CB$ and $N$ the midpoint of $DE$. It has been shown that the diagonals $OF$ and $CE$ bisect each other, at the point with position vector $\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c+\mathbf d)$, where $\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{OA}$, $\mathbf c=\overrightarrow{OC}$, $\mathbf d=\overrightarrow{OD}$. Prove that the midpoint of $MN$ is the point where the diagonals $OF$ and $CE$ intersect.
questions.answer:
Since $\overrightarrow{CB}=\overrightarrow{DE}=\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf a$: $\overrightarrow{OM}=\mathbf c+\tfrac12\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{ON}=\mathbf d+\tfrac12\mathbf a$. The midpoint $Z$ of $MN$ has
$$\overrightarrow{OZ}=\tfrac12\left(\mathbf c+\tfrac12\mathbf a+\mathbf d+\tfrac12\mathbf a\right)=\tfrac12(\mathbf a+\mathbf c+\mathbf d),$$
the same as the intersection point of $OF$ and $CE$.

questions.question: Prove that for $a,b\in\mathbb R^+$, $\dfrac{a+b}2\ge\sqrt{ab}$.
questions.answer: $(\sqrt a-\sqrt b)^2\ge0\Rightarrow a-2\sqrt{ab}+b\ge0\Rightarrow\dfrac{a+b}{2}\ge\sqrt{ab}$.

questions.question:
Given that $\dfrac{a+b}2\ge\sqrt{ab}$ for all $a,b\in\mathbb R^+$, prove that for $a,b\in\mathbb R^+$
$$\sqrt{ab}\ge\frac{2}{\frac1a+\frac1b}.$$
questions.answer: Apply the given result to $\frac1a$ and $\frac1b$: $\dfrac{\frac1a+\frac1b}{2}\ge\sqrt{\dfrac1{ab}}=\dfrac1{\sqrt{ab}}$. Taking reciprocals of both (positive) sides reverses the inequality: $\dfrac{2}{\frac1a+\frac1b}\le\sqrt{ab}$.

questions.question:
Prove that for $a,b\in\mathbb R^+$
$$\frac{2}{\frac1a+\frac1b}\le\sqrt{ab}\le\frac{a+b}2\le\sqrt{\frac{a^2+b^2}2}.$$
(You may use that $\dfrac{a+b}2\ge\sqrt{ab}$ and $\sqrt{ab}\ge\dfrac2{\frac1a+\frac1b}$ for positive $a,b$.)
questions.answer: The first two inequalities are the given results. For the last: $(a-b)^2\ge0\Rightarrow a^2+b^2\ge2ab\Rightarrow2(a^2+b^2)\ge(a+b)^2\Rightarrow\dfrac{a^2+b^2}{2}\ge\left(\dfrac{a+b}2\right)^2$. Both sides are positive and $\sqrt{\ }$ is increasing, so $\sqrt{\dfrac{a^2+b^2}2}\ge\dfrac{a+b}2$. Chaining the inequalities gives the result.

questions.question:
Using the inequality $\dfrac{2}{\frac1a+\frac1b}\le\dfrac{a+b}{2}$ (valid for all $a,b\in\mathbb R^+$), or otherwise, prove that for $x,y,z\in\mathbb R^+$:
$$\frac1{x+y}+\frac1{y+z}+\frac1{z+x}\le\frac12\left(\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z\right).$$
questions.answer:
With $a=x$, $b=y$: $\dfrac{2xy}{x+y}\le\dfrac{x+y}2$, so (reciprocating) $\dfrac{x+y}{2xy}\ge\dfrac2{x+y}$, i.e. $\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1y+\dfrac1x\right)\ge\dfrac{2}{x+y}$, giving
$$\frac1{x+y}\le\frac14\left(\frac1x+\frac1y\right).$$
Similarly $\dfrac1{y+z}\le\dfrac14\left(\dfrac1y+\dfrac1z\right)$ and $\dfrac1{z+x}\le\dfrac14\left(\dfrac1z+\dfrac1x\right)$. Adding:
$$\frac1{x+y}+\frac1{y+z}+\frac1{z+x}\le\frac14\left(\frac2x+\frac2y+\frac2z\right)=\frac12\left(\frac1x+\frac1y+\frac1z\right).$$

questions.question:
By considering the function $y=\sqrt x$ from $x=0$ to $x=n+1$, use $n+1$ applications of the trapezoidal rule to show that
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sqrt k<\frac{(4n+1)\sqrt{n+1}}{6}.$$
questions.answer:
Divide $[0,n+1]$ into $n+1$ strips of width $1$ with ordinates $\sqrt0,\sqrt1,\dots,\sqrt{n+1}$. Since $y=\sqrt x$ is concave down, each trapezium lies under the curve, so the trapezoidal rule underestimates the integral:
$$\frac12\Big[\sqrt0+\sqrt{n+1}+2\big(\sqrt1+\sqrt2+\dots+\sqrt n\big)\Big]<\int_0^{n+1}\sqrt x\,dx=\tfrac23(n+1)^{3/2}.$$
So $\sum_{k=1}^n\sqrt k<\tfrac23(n+1)^{3/2}-\tfrac12\sqrt{n+1}=\dfrac{4(n+1)\sqrt{n+1}-3\sqrt{n+1}}{6}=\dfrac{(4n+1)\sqrt{n+1}}6.$

questions.question:
Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{(1-x^2)^n}\,dx$. Show that for integers $n\ge2$,
$$I_n=\frac{n}{n+1}I_{n-2}.$$
Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{(1-x^2)^n}\,dx$, and given that $I_n=\dfrac n{n+1}I_{n-2}$ for integers $n\ge2$, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{(1-x^2)^5}\,dx$.
questions.answer: $I_1=\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx=\dfrac\pi4$ (area of a quarter of the unit circle). Then $I_3=\tfrac34I_1=\dfrac{3\pi}{16}$ and $I_5=\tfrac56I_3=\dfrac{5\pi}{32}$.

questions.question:
Gabbro's rocket ship, of mass $m$ kilograms, is initially stationary on the surface of his home planet. The engines deliver a constant upward force of $F$ newtons. Up to a height of $h$ metres above the surface the ship experiences a constant gravitational acceleration $g$ m s$^{-2}$ and an air resistance of $50\%$ of the square of the ship's velocity (i.e. $0.5v^2$ newtons).

Show that when Gabbro has reached a height of $h$ metres he is travelling at a speed of
$$\sqrt{2(F-mg)\left(1-e^{-\frac hm}\right)}\ \text{ metres per second.}$$
questions.answer:
Taking up as positive, $ma=F-mg-0.5v^2$, so $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac{F-mg-0.5v^2}{m}$ and $\dfrac{dx}{dv}=\dfrac{mv}{F-mg-0.5v^2}$. Then
$$\int_0^hdx=\int_0^v\frac{mv}{F-mg-0.5v^2}dv\ \Rightarrow\ h=-m\Big[\ln\left|F-mg-0.5v^2\right|\Big]_0^v=-m\ln\frac{F-mg-0.5v^2}{F-mg}.$$
So $\dfrac{F-mg-0.5v^2}{F-mg}=e^{-h/m}$, giving $0.5v^2=(F-mg)\left(1-e^{-h/m}\right)$ and (as $v>0$) $v=\sqrt{2(F-mg)\left(1-e^{-h/m}\right)}$.

questions.question: The gravitational acceleration of a ship near a planet of radius $R$ is inversely proportional to the square of its distance from the centre of the planet, and equals $g$ at the surface. Show that when the ship is at height $x$ above the surface, the gravity has magnitude $\dfrac{gR^2}{(R+x)^2}$ metres per second squared.
questions.answer: The distance from the centre is $R+x$, so the magnitude is $\dfrac k{(R+x)^2}$. At the surface ($x=0$) it equals $g$: $g=\dfrac k{R^2}\Rightarrow k=gR^2$. Hence the gravity is $\dfrac{gR^2}{(R+x)^2}$.

questions.question:
Gabbro's rocket ship, of mass $m$ kilograms, is initially stationary on the surface of his home planet. The engines deliver a constant upward force of $F$ newtons. Up to a height of $h$ metres above the surface the ship experiences a constant gravitational acceleration $g$ m s$^{-2}$ and an air resistance of $50\%$ of the square of the ship's velocity (i.e. $0.5v^2$ newtons).
At height $h$ the engines are turned off and air resistance becomes negligible. Above this height the only force on the ship is gravity, of magnitude $\dfrac{gR^2}{(R+x)^2}$ where $R$ is the radius of the planet and $x$ the height above the surface. Using the result that the speed at height $h$ is $\sqrt{2(F-mg)\left(1-e^{-h/m}\right)}$, show that for the ship to escape (never return), the force of the engines must exceed the weight of the ship by
$$\frac{gR^2}{(h+R)\left(1-e^{-h/m}\right)}\ \text{newtons.}$$
questions.answer:
Let $u$ be the speed at height $h$. Above $h$, taking up as positive, $v\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-\dfrac{gR^2}{(R+x)^2}$, so
$$\int_u^vv\,dv=-gR^2\int_h^x\frac{dx}{(R+x)^2}\ \Rightarrow\ \tfrac12v^2-\tfrac12u^2=gR^2\left(\frac1{R+x}-\frac1{R+h}\right).$$
Thus $v^2=u^2-2gR^2\left(\dfrac1{R+h}-\dfrac1{R+x}\right)$. Since the acceleration is always negative, the ship escapes only if $v^2>0$ for all $x$; as $x\to\infty$ this requires $u^2>\dfrac{2gR^2}{R+h}$.

Substituting $u^2=2(F-mg)\left(1-e^{-h/m}\right)$:
$$2(F-mg)\left(1-e^{-h/m}\right)>\frac{2gR^2}{h+R}\ \Rightarrow\ F-mg>\frac{gR^2}{(h+R)\left(1-e^{-h/m}\right)}.$$
Since $mg$ is the weight of the ship, the engine force must exceed the weight by this amount.

questions.question:
Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\frac{\ln(x+1)}{x^2+1}\,dx$.

(You may quote the identity $\displaystyle\int_0^af(x)\,dx=\int_0^af(a-x)\,dx$ without proof at any point in your working.)
questions.answer:
Let $x=\tan u$, $dx=\sec^2u\,du$; limits $0\to\frac\pi4$:
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\ln(\tan u+1)}{\sec^2u}\sec^2u\,du=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan u)\,du.$$
Apply the identity: 
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln\left(1+\tan\left(\tfrac\pi4-u\right)\right)du=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln\left(1+\frac{1-\tan u}{1+\tan u}\right)du=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln\frac2{1+\tan u}\,du$$
$$=\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln2\,du-\int_0^{\pi/4}\ln(1+\tan u)\,du=\frac\pi4\ln2-I.$$
So $2I=\dfrac\pi4\ln2$ and $I=\dfrac\pi8\ln2$.

questions.question: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $|z|=1$ and $z^{n+1}-z^n-1=0$. Prove that $n+2$ is a multiple of $6$.
questions.answer:
From $z^n(z-1)=1$ and $|z|=1$: $|z-1|=1$. So $z$ lies on both $|z|=1$ and $|z-1|=1$; the triangle with vertices $0$, $1$, $z$ is equilateral, so $z=\cos\frac\pi3\pm i\sin\frac\pi3$, i.e. $\arg z=\pm\frac\pi3$. Then $z^3=\cos(\pm\pi)=-1$, so $z^3+1=(z+1)(z^2-z+1)=0$ and since $z\ne-1$, $z^2-z+1=0$, i.e. $z^2=z-1$. Substituting into $z^n(z-1)=1$: $z^{n+2}=1$.

By de Moivre, $z^{n+2}=\cos\left(\pm\frac{(n+2)\pi}3\right)+i\sin\left(\pm\frac{(n+2)\pi}3\right)=1$ requires $\frac{(n+2)\pi}{3}=2\pi k$ for an integer $k$, so $n+2=6k$: a multiple of $6$.

(The school's working ends by noting $z^6=1$ so $z^{6k}=1$ and concludes $n+2=6k$; that step is the converse of what is needed. The argument above uses $\arg z=\pm\frac\pi3$ to justify it. The school's working also used exponential form $e^{\pm i\pi/3}$, which is rewritten here in polar form.)

questions.question: Coprime integers share no common factor other than $1$. If $a$ and $b$ are coprime and $ax=by$, show that $a$ is a factor of $y$, for integers $a,b,x,y$.
questions.answer: $ax=by$, so $\dfrac xy=\dfrac ba$ (for $y\ne 0$). Since $a$ and $b$ are coprime, $\dfrac ba$ is in lowest terms, so any other representation of this ratio has the form $\dfrac xy=\dfrac{kb}{ka}$ for an integer $k$. Hence $y=ka$ and $a$ is a factor of $y$. (If $y=0$ then $a$ divides $y$ trivially.)

questions.question:
Coprime integers share no common factor other than $1$. You may use that if $a$ and $b$ are coprime and $ax=by$ then $a$ is a factor of $y$.

$P(x)=a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+a_1x+a_0$ is a polynomial of degree $n$ with integer coefficients. Let a rational root of $P(x)$ be written $\dfrac pq$ where $p$ and $q$ are coprime integers (so $p^n$ and $q$ are also coprime). Prove that $q$ is a factor of $a_n$.
questions.answer:
$P\!\left(\tfrac pq\right)=0$; multiply by $q^n$: $a_np^n+a_{n-1}p^{n-1}q+\dots+a_1pq^{n-1}+a_0q^n=0$. Hence
$$a_np^n=q\left(-a_{n-1}p^{n-1}-a_{n-2}p^{n-2}q-\dots-a_0q^{n-1}\right).$$
This has the form $q\cdot X=p^n\cdot a_n$ with $q$ and $p^n$ coprime, so by part (i) $q$ is a factor of $a_n$.

questions.question:
Letting $\cos\theta=x$, we can write cos$(n\theta)$ as a polynomial in $x$:
$\cos0\theta=1$, $\cos\theta=x$, $\cos2\theta=2x^2-1$, $\cos3\theta=4x^3-3x$, $\cos4\theta=8x^4-8x^2+1$, $\dots$

By considering the first few terms in the expansion of $(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^n$, or otherwise, show that the leading coefficient of the polynomial expansion of $\cos n\theta$ in $x$ is $2^{n-1}$ (for $n\ge1$).
questions.answer:
Let $c=\cos\theta$, $s=\sin\theta$. By de Moivre and the binomial theorem, equating real parts:
$$\cos n\theta=\binom n0c^n-\binom n2c^{n-2}s^2+\binom n4c^{n-4}s^4-\dots$$
Replace $s^2=1-c^2$: the $k$-th even term is $(-1)^k\binom n{2k}c^{n-2k}(1-c^2)^k$, whose leading term is $(-1)^k\binom n{2k}c^{n-2k}(-c^2)^k=\binom n{2k}c^n$. So the coefficient of $c^n=x^n$ is
$$\binom n0+\binom n2+\binom n4+\dots.$$
From $(1+t)^n$ at $t=1$ and $t=-1$: $2^n=\sum\binom nk$ and $0=\sum(-1)^k\binom nk$. Adding: $2^n=2\left[\binom n0+\binom n2+\dots\right]$, so the sum of the even-indexed binomial coefficients is $2^{n-1}$. So the leading coefficient is $2^{n-1}$.

questions.question:
Let $n$ be an odd integer with $n\ge3$ and suppose $\cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac1{\sqrt n}\right)=k\pi$. Prove that $k$ is irrational.

You may use: (1) if $p$ and $q$ are coprime integers and $\dfrac pq$ is a rational root of a polynomial with integer coefficients, then $q$ divides the leading coefficient; (2) $\cos(m\theta)$ is a polynomial in $x=\cos\theta$ with integer coefficients and leading coefficient $2^{m-1}$ (for integers $m\ge1$).
questions.answer:
Suppose, for contradiction, that $k=\dfrac pq$ is rational ($p,q$ positive integers). Let $\alpha=k\pi$, so $\cos\alpha=\dfrac1{\sqrt n}$ and $\cos^2\alpha=\dfrac1n$. Then $\dfrac1n=\dfrac12+\dfrac12\cos2\alpha$, so
$$\cos2\alpha=\frac2n-1=\frac{2-n}{n}.$$
As $n$ is odd, $\gcd(2-n,n)=\gcd(2,n)=1$, so this fraction is in lowest terms.

Now $2\alpha=\dfrac{2p\pi}{q}$, so $q\cdot2\alpha=2p\pi$ and $\cos(q\cdot2\alpha)=1$. Writing $x=\cos2\alpha$, $\cos(q\cdot2\alpha)=T(x)$ where $T$ is an integer-coefficient polynomial of degree $q$ with leading coefficient $2^{q-1}$. So $x=\dfrac{2-n}{n}$ is a rational root of $T(x)-1=0$, a polynomial with integer coefficients and leading coefficient $2^{q-1}$. By (1), the denominator $n$ divides $2^{q-1}$. But $n$ is odd and $n\ge3$, so $n$ cannot divide a power of $2$. This is a contradiction, hence $k$ is irrational.
